nameStory: Powell's amaranth is named after John Wesley Powell, the famous 19th-century explorer and geologist who led the first expedition down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon. This hardy plant was first scientifically described from the southwestern United States where Powell conducted much of his groundbreaking exploration work. Like its namesake explorer, this amaranth has proven to be quite the traveler, spreading far beyond its native range.
description: Powell's amaranth is a tall, weedy annual plant that can grow 2-6 feet high with a sturdy, upright stem. It produces dense clusters of tiny greenish flowers that form thick, bristly spikes at the top of the plant and along the branches. The leaves are oval-shaped with pointed tips and can feel slightly rough to the touch. This is one of many amaranth species that have spread well beyond their original homes to become common weeds in disturbed soils.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, bristly flower spikes that feel rough and prickly when touched, with tiny greenish flowers packed tightly together in thick clusters at stem tips and branch ends

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with pointed tips, alternate arrangement on stems, often with a slightly rough texture and prominent veins that you can feel when rubbing the leaf surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy annual that grows upright like a small green tower, often branching in the upper portions to create a somewhat bushy appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, shiny black seeds that fall easily from the mature flower spikes when shaken or brushed against

habitat: Powell's amaranth thrives in disturbed soils like garden edges, vacant lots, roadsides, and agricultural areas throughout New England. It prefers sunny locations with rich, moist soil but can tolerate poor conditions. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy plants in areas where the ground has been recently disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate when soil warms in late spring, producing small seedlings with the characteristic oval leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and begin flowering in mid to late summer, developing their distinctive bristly flower spikes.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes mature and release countless tiny black seeds before the plant dies with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stalks may persist into winter, but the annual plant has completed its life cycle.

funFact: A single Powell's amaranth plant can produce over 100,000 seeds in one growing season, and those seeds can remain viable in the soil for decades, waiting for the right conditions to sprout - which explains how this southwestern native has conquered disturbed soils across the continent!
confusionNotes: Powell's amaranth is easily confused with redroot amaranth, but redroot has a distinctive reddish taproot (hence the name) and rougher, more hairy leaves. A simple memory trick: if you can pull up the plant and see red on the roots, it's redroot amaranth; if the roots are whitish, it's likely Powell's amaranth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'green amaranth' sometimes, this name is also used for Amaranthus viridis, which can cause confusion. Powell's amaranth is also sometimes lumped together with other amaranths under the general term 'pigweed,' an old common name that refers to several amaranth species that were once fed to pigs.
compareHints: Powell's amaranth differs from redroot amaranth by lacking the red-tinged roots and having less hairy leaves. Unlike smooth pigweed, Powell's amaranth has rougher-textured flower spikes that feel more bristly to the touch. It's generally taller and more robust than purple amaranth, and lacks the spines found on spiny amaranth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England amaranths, redroot is distinguished by its reddish taproot and compact, bristly flower clusters.
Unlike the weedy Redroot Amaranth found in gardens and fields, Tidalmarsh Amaranth is strictly a coastal specialist that grows much taller and in dense colonies.

Purple amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives by its distinctly prostrate, mat-forming growth habit - while redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed grow upright like small bushes, purple amaranth sprawls along the ground.
Among its amaranth relatives, red amaranth stands out for its particularly robust, upright growth and thick, erect flower spikes.
Love-lies-bleeding stands out dramatically from its wild amaranth relatives in New England because of its long, pendulous flower clusters - all the others have upright, spike-like flower heads.
Compared to redroot amaranth, smooth pigweed has less hairy stems and leaves, and its flower spikes tend to be more upright rather than drooping.
Among the New England amaranths, rough-fruit amaranth stands out for its preference for wetter habitats and its distinctively bumpy seeds.
Among New England's amaranths, green amaranth is unique for maintaining its green color throughout the season - most others develop reddish or purplish tones in stems, roots, or flower clusters.
Among New England's amaranths, spiny amaranth is the only one with actual spines - species like redroot amaranth and smooth pigweed may have bristly flowers but lack the sharp spines at leaf bases.
Palmer's Amaranth stands out from its amaranth relatives because it's 'dioecious' - meaning individual plants are either male or female, not both like most other amaranths.
Unlike its weedy cousins like Redroot Amaranth that grow tall and upright in disturbed soils, Seabeach Amaranth stays flat against the sand and has much thicker, more succulent leaves and stems.
